title: Λύκος καὶ ὄνος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 228. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος τῶν λοιπῶν στρατηγήσας λύκων νόμους ἔταξε πᾶσιν, ἵνα ὅ τι ἂν ἕκαστος κυνηγήσῃ, πάντα εἰς μέσον ἄξῃ καὶ μερίδα ἴσην ἑκάστῳ δώσῃ, ὅπως μὴ οἱ λοιποὶ ἐνδεεῖς ὄντες ἀλλήλους κατεσθίωσιν.
sentences.tr: Lykos tōn loipōn stratēgēsas lykōn nomous etaxe pasin, hina ho ti an hekastos kynēgēsēi, panta eis meson axēi kai merida isēn hekastōi dōsēi, hopōs mē hoi loipoi endeeis ontes allēlous katesthiōsin.
sentences.l: A wolf, having become general of the rest of the wolves, laid down laws for all, that whatever each should hunt, he should bring it all into the middle and give an equal portion to each, so that the rest, being in want, should not devour one another.
sentences.i: A wolf who had taken command of the other wolves laid down laws for them all: whatever each of them hunted down he was to bring the whole of it into the common stock and give an equal share to each, so that the rest should not, in their want, eat one another.
sentences.n: στρατηγέω takes the genitive of those one commands. εἰς μέσον, 'into the middle,' is the common store, what is set out for everyone to divide. The relative clause is indefinite — ὅ τι ἄν with the subjunctive, 'whatever he may hunt' — and πάντα then picks it up again loosely, 'all of it'; the Greek restates rather than subordinates.

sentences.t: Ὄνος δὲ παρελθὼν τὴν χαίτην σείσας ἔφη· « Ἐκ φρενὸς λύκου καλὴ γνώμη· ἀλλὰ πῶς σὺ τὴν χθεσινὴν ἄγραν τῇ κοίτῃ ἐναπέθου ;
sentences.tr: Onos de parelthōn tēn chaitēn seisas ephē· « Ek phrenos lykou kalē gnōmē· alla pōs sy tēn chthesinēn agran tēi koitēi enapethou ;
sentences.l: But an ass, having come forward and having shaken his mane, said: « A fine judgement, out of a wolf's mind; but how is it that you laid away yesterday's catch in your lair?
sentences.i: But an ass came forward, shook his mane and said: « A noble resolution, from a wolf's mind — but how came you to stow yesterday's catch away in your lair?
sentences.n: Two aorist participles for the two gestures, then the verb: the ass comes forward, tosses his mane, and speaks. The praise is said dryly and taken back at once by ἀλλά. ἐναπέθου is second singular aorist middle of ἐναποτίθημι, to put a thing away in a place for oneself — the middle is what convicts him.

sentences.l: Bring this into the middle, portioning it out. »
sentences.i: Bring it into the common stock and share it out. »
sentences.n: ἄγε here is the full verb 'bring,' not the mere interjection 'come now': it answers εἰς μέσον ἄξῃ in the law the wolf himself made. The aorist participle ἀπομερίσας is coincident with the imperative, not prior to it — the dividing is part of the bringing. Chambry begins a new sentence after the question mark, and the capital Ἄγε is why.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐλεγχθεὶς τοὺς νόμους ἀνέλυσεν.
sentences.tr: Ho de elenchtheis tous nomous anelysen.
sentences.l: And he, having been shown up, dissolved the laws.
sentences.n: ἐλεγχθείς is the aorist passive of the same ἐλέγχω that closes fable 227 — to be put to the proof and found out. ἀναλύω is to loose what has been bound: the laws are untied as knots are.

sentences.t: Ὅτι αὐτοὶ οἱ τοὺς νόμους δικαίως ὁρίζειν δοκοῦντες καὶ ἐν οἷς ὁρίζουσιν καὶ δικάζουσιν οὐκ ἐμμένουσιν.
sentences.tr: Hoti autoi hoi tous nomous dikaiōs horizein dokountes kai en hois horizousin kai dikazousin ouk emmenousin.
sentences.l: That the very men who seem to lay down the laws justly do not themselves abide in the things in which they ordain and give judgement.
sentences.i: The story shows that the very men who seem to lay down the laws justly do not themselves abide by the rules they ordain and judge by.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἐμμένω takes ἐν with the dative, 'stand fast in, abide by.' The relative ἐν οἷς has swallowed its antecedent — 'in those things in which' — and αὐτοί sharpens the point to the lawgivers themselves.
